title: Continual Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models by Suppressing Cross-Edit Interference

paper.title: Continual Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models by Suppressing Cross-Edit Interference
paper.abstract: Abstract Concept erasure removes copyright-protected, privacy-sensitive, or otherwise undesirable concepts from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models to support content governance and compliance. As erasure requests arrive over time, models must remove new targets without undoing prior erasures. Existing methods do not constrain interference across edits: residual perturbations outside the retain set interact and accumulate, degrading unrelated generations and sometimes collapsing previously erased targets into noise. We propose CEASE ( C ontinual E rasure via A daptive S ubspace E diting), a training-free method that imposes two subspace constraints on a closed-form solver. CEASE adds the token representation of the shared replacement to the solver’s invariance matrix and, when interference is detected, projects the current update onto the orthogonal complement of dominant output directions extracted from cumulative past updates. A closed-form decomposition attributes the accumulated interference to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions, showing that the two constraints suppress these respective sources. Across continual erasure of celebrities, artistic styles, and instances, CEASE achieves the most consistent erase--preserve trade-off, while existing methods either degrade general generation or insufficiently erase targets. 1 1 1 Project page: https://continual-erasure.cvmlgroup.web.illinois.edu/

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Concept erasure aims to remove copyright-protected, privacy-sensitive, or otherwise undesirable concepts from pretrained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models, making it an important tool for content governance and compliance Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2025) . In practice, new erasure targets arrive over time Lee et al. (2026) ; George et al. (2025) , extending concept erasure from one-shot to continual editing: the model must remove new targets without allowing later updates to undo prior erasures or degrade generation of unrelated concepts. Prior studies report that retained model utility declines when erasure requests are processed sequentially Lee et al. (2026) ; George et al. (2025) . In our experiments, sequentially applying standard erasure methods Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2026) reveals two related failure modes. First, general generation quality declines on prompts unrelated to any erased concept. Second, outputs for some erased targets become incoherent instead of reflecting the prescribed replacement ( e.g. “a person” for a celebrity). Each edit explicitly protects only a finite retain set Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2026) and can therefore perturb embeddings outside it Wuerkaixi et al. (2025) ; Thakral et al. (2025) . These perturbations interact and accumulate across successive updates, making it difficult for existing methods Li et al. (2026) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) to confine the effects of erasure to the target concepts. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), COCO FID on unrelated prompts rises as the number of edits increases Lin et al. (2014) . This exposes a limitation of existing preservation constraints in the continual setting: protecting a finite retain set at each step does not reliably prevent subsequent updates from cumulatively degrading general generation. Beyond image quality, this degradation also weakens the model’s ability to follow prompt semantics: Figure 1 (b) shows that, after 100 edits, the CLIP score on the same prompts falls well below that of the unedited model. This reduced ability to follow prompt semantics may also affect the outcomes of previous erasures, because the replacement outputs for earlier targets depend on the same continually updated weights. Figure 1 (c) illustrates both effects in the baseline models: they corrupt an unrelated scene and produce noise for the erased celebrity, failing to generate the prescribed generic portrait. Figure 1: Utility loss under continual celebrity erasure. (a) COCO FID on 1,000 unrelated prompts as the number of erased concepts grows from 10 to 100; lower is better. (b) COCO CLIP score on the same prompts after 100 edits; the dashed line marks the unedited model. (c) Generations after 100 edits for an unrelated COCO scene (top) and the erased target “Tom Cruise” (bottom). To suppress the accumulation of interference in continual concept erasure, we propose CEASE ( C ontinual E rasure via A daptive S ubspace E diting), a training-free method based on two subspace constraints. CEASE adds the token representation of the shared replacement to the invariance matrix of the closed-form solver, preventing subsequent updates from modifying this representation. It also extracts the dominant output directions from cumulative past updates and, when interference is detected, projects the current update onto their orthogonal complement. Theoretically, a closed-form decomposition attributes the accumulated interference to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions, and shows that the two designs suppress the respective sources. Empirically, CEASE maintains stable COCO FID throughout the edit sequence and a COCO CLIP score close to the unedited reference after 100 edits, as shown in Fig. 1 (a) and (b). Across continual erasure tasks involving celebrities, artistic styles, and instances, CEASE achieves the most consistent erase–preserve trade-off. On style erasure, CEASE reduces COCO FID by 73% relative to the strongest prior method. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We formalize how interference accumulates across edits in continual concept erasure, and derive a closed-form decomposition that attributes it to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions. • We introduce two training-free subspace constraints: one keeps the token representation of the shared replacement invariant, while the other steers the current update away from the dominant output directions of past edits, thereby suppressing the two interference sources. • We evaluate continual erasure of celebrities, artistic styles, and instances across multiple diffusion backbones and assess both erasure and preservation; CEASE achieves the best erase–preserve balance among the compared methods while keeping retained concepts recognizable at rates close to the reference model.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models. Text-to-image diffusion models Zhang et al. (2023a) ; Ma et al. (2024) ; Ji et al. (2026) trained on uncurated web data can reproduce copyrighted styles, recognizable identities, and other undesired content, and concept erasure removes such targets from a pretrained model after training. Existing methods fall into three families. Training-based methods fine-tune the model with a concept-suppression objective and a preservation regularizer Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2024) ; Kumari et al. (2023) ; Huang et al. (2024) ; Lyu et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Kim et al. (2024) ; Zhao et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2025) , with a separate strand hardening the erasure against adversarial prompts Fan et al. (2024) ; Heng and Soh (2023) ; Pham et al. (2024) ; Park et al. (2024) ; their common cost is that each new target requires another fine-tuning loop. Editing-based methods instead update cross-attention projections through a closed-form least-squares solution, from TIME Orgad et al. (2023) and UCE Gandikota et al. (2024) to MACE Lu et al. (2024) , RECE Gong et al. (2024) , and SPEED Li et al. (2026) ; they edit the model in seconds, but their preservation depends on a finite retain set. Non-parametric methods leave the weights untouched and intervene at sampling time Schramowski et al. (2023) ; Das et al. (2024) ; Rando et al. (2022) . All three families are typically evaluated with the full target set known before editing; our study instead evaluates repeated application to an already-edited model. Sequential Unlearning. Sequential unlearning is closely related to continual learning and online learning Liu et al. (2020) ; Liu et al. (2021a) ; Liu et al. (2021b) ; Liu et al. (2023a) ; Liu et al. (2023b) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2019) ; Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Fischer et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2023b) . While continual learning and online learning typically focus on acquiring new knowledge without forgetting, sequential unlearning poses the complementary challenge of repeatedly removing targeted knowledge without causing unintended forgetting of retained concepts. In deployment, takedown demands and right-to-be-forgotten obligations arrive as a stream. For language models, the locate-then-edit paradigm Meng et al. (2022a) ; Meng et al. (2022b) degrades under repeated application, and mitigations include drift-restraining regularizers Ma et al. (2025) ; Gu et al. (2024) , external edit memories Hartvigsen et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2024b) , and projections onto the null space of preserved keys Fang et al. (2025) ; these approaches operate on factual associations, where edits do not share a common redirection target. For diffusion models, Selective Amnesia Heng and Soh (2023) first cast concept forgetting as a continual-learning problem, and later work adds concept-aware masking with distillation Li et al. (2025) , gradient projection against semantically related concepts Lee et al. (2026) , and multi-objective distillation across deletion requests George et al. (2025) ; these methods suppress the degradation as a monolithic quantity without analyzing where it comes from. In contrast, we approach continual erasure from the perspective of cross-edit interference: we trace the failure to the interference that successive edits accumulate on unprotected prompts, and design our method to suppress this interference.

sections.heading: 3 Analysis and Method
sections.text: Section 3.1 defines the continual erasure problem and the base closed-form update. Section 3.2 then explains why update noise accumulates under sequential editing. Guided by the two sources identified in this analysis, Sec. 3.3 presents CEASE.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Baselines and Benchmarks. We evaluate on three concept erasure benchmarks adapted from MACE Lu et al. (2024) and SPEED Li et al. (2026) , covering celebrities, artistic styles, and object or character instances. Each benchmark pairs 100 erased concepts with 100 disjoint retained concepts and uses five prompt templates per concept. We compare two groups of baselines: standard erasure methods, comprising the closed-form SPEED Li et al. (2026) , UCE Gandikota et al. (2024) , and RECE Gong et al. (2024) and the training-based ESD Gandikota et al. (2023) and ConAbl Kumari et al. (2023) , and continual-unlearning methods, comprising CUIG-GradProj Lee et al. (2026) and Sculpting Memory Li et al. (2025) . Metrics. We report CLIP score (CS) ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) for image–prompt alignment, and FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for the distribution-level and image-level distance from the unedited backbone’s generations, on each of the erase set, the retain set, and 1,000 MS-COCO captions. On the erase and retain sets we add one task-matched fourth metric. For celebrities, Acc is the recognition accuracy of an open-ended VLM judge (Qwen2-VL-7B) Wang et al. (2024a) asked to name the person in the image; for instances, Acc is the CLIP zero-shot top-1 accuracy against the 200 concept candidates; both should drop on the erase set and stay high on the retain set. For styles, the LAION aesthetic score (Aes) ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) is a no-reference quality rating on a 1–10 scale that should stay near the unedited reference. Implementation Details. The main experiments use Stable Diffusion v1.4 with DPM-Solver sampling and classifier-free guidance 7.5 Rombach et al. (2021) . The per-task anchors are “person” for celebrities, “art” for styles, and “object” for instances. All experiments run on a single H100 GPU. Additional implementation details, including hyperparameters, are provided in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied continual concept erasure, where deletion requests arrive one after another and each edit builds on all previous ones. We traced the severe degradation of existing methods in this regime to accumulating cross-edit interference, and proposed CEASE, a training-free framework that protects the shared anchor and steers each new update away from the directions perturbed by past edits. Experiments on erasing celebrities, artistic styles, and instances across multiple backbones show that CEASE achieves the most consistent erase–preserve trade-off. Limitations. First, our experiments focus on the Stable Diffusion family, and extending CEASE to more recent architectures such as FLUX is a natural next step. Second, this work instantiates the proposed constraints in a closed-form solver, and generalizing them to training-based erasure methods is left to future work. Third, our sequences contain up to 100 edits; evaluating substantially longer streams is conceptually straightforward but computationally expensive, since every additional step requires regenerating and re-evaluating thousands of images.

sections.heading: A.1 Implementation Details
sections.text: ESD Gandikota et al. (2023) uses the ESD-x variant, fine-tuning the cross-attention projections under the negative-guidance objective for 200 Adam iterations per step at learning rate 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} with guidance strength 1.0, and training latents are generated at guidance 3.0 over 50 DDIM steps. ConAbl Kumari et al. (2023) fine-tunes the cross-attention weights toward its own anchor-prompt prediction, with prior-loss weight 1.0 and 100 Adam iterations per concept at learning rate 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} . UCE Gandikota et al. (2024) applies one closed-form least-squares update per step to the key and value projections, with erase scale 1.0, preserve scale 1.0, and regularization λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 . RECE Gong et al. (2024) alternates a closed-form value edit with the derivation of an adversarial target embedding, in the replace regime with 3 adversarial epochs, erase scale 1.0, preserve scale 0.1, closed-form λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 , and adversarial regularization 0.1. SPEED Li et al. (2026) redirects each target to the anchor while projecting the update onto the null space of an augmented retain set; its invariance matrix uses the empty-prompt representation, and CEASE’s AIC additionally inserts the task anchor. Both use null-space threshold 0.1, retain scale 0.05, λ = 0 \lambda=0 , 10 augmented retain samples per concept, and the official multi-concept configuration without the importance-based retain filter. CUIG-GradProj Lee et al. (2026) adds the official semantic-aware gradient-projection regularizer to ConAbl with 200 auxiliary prompts, fine-tuning the key and value projections with batch size 4, learning rate 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} before the official scaling, 500 warmup steps, and weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} , for 2,000 iterations per request (1,000 for style). Sculpting Memory Li et al. (2025) combines a dynamic parameter mask with distillation from the preceding model, using 100 generated images per path, batch size 2, 10 epochs, learning rate 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} , and a cosine OneCycle schedule with 50 warmup steps; the mask updates every 100 steps with fraction 0.5, and the unlearning and distillation scales are 0.25.

sections.text: Fig. 6 compares single-request wall time on one H100 GPU. sections.heading: A.7 Additional Qualitative Comparisons
sections.text: This section provides qualitative comparisons beyond the single case shown in the main text. Fig. 7 extends the main-text comparison to four cases per category on the celebrity task, Figs. 8 and 9 give the same comparison on the style and instance tasks, and Figs. 10 and 11 repeat the celebrity comparison on the Stable Diffusion v1.5 and v2.1 backbones. Every figure follows the same layout: columns show the unedited reference followed by ESD, UCE, ConAbl, RECE, SPEED, CUIG-GradProj, Sculpting Memory, and CEASE after the full 100-step sequence, and the three row blocks show four cases each of erased targets, retained concepts, and unrelated MS-COCO prompts. The failure modes match the quantitative results and the main-text analysis. On the erased rows, CEASE redirects each target to a coherent anchor substitute, whereas ESD often leaves the erased identity or style still recognizable, and RECE, UCE, and CUIG-GradProj collapse to noise-like textures once the sequence is long. Sculpting Memory remains photorealistic but drifts to subjects unrelated to either the target or its anchor. On the retained and COCO rows, the picture inverts: the destructive baselines corrupt concepts they were never asked to erase, SPEED preserves some cases but degrades others as its accumulated interference grows, and CEASE stays visually closest to the reference across both row blocks. The v1.5 and v2.1 figures show the same pattern, confirming that these behaviors are properties of the continual setting rather than of the v1.4 backbone. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.01989v1 [cs.CV] 01 Oct 2026 Continual Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models by Suppressing Cross-Edit Interference Yongliang Wu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Haori Lu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Jinqi Luo Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Wei Cao Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Xingyu Zhu † † thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: National University of Singapore Yaoyao Liu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Abstract Concept erasure removes copyright-protected, privacy-sensitive, or otherwise undesirable concepts from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models to support content governance and compliance. As erasure requests arrive over time, models must remove new targets without undoing prior erasures. Existing methods do not constrain interference across edits: residual perturbations outside the retain set interact and accumulate, degrading unrelated generations and sometimes collapsing previously erased targets into noise. We propose CEASE ( C ontinual E rasure via A daptive S ubspace E diting), a training-free method that imposes two subspace constraints on a closed-form solver. CEASE adds the token representation of the shared replacement to the solver’s invariance matrix and, when interference is detected, projects the current update onto the orthogonal complement of dominant output directions extracted from cumulative past updates. A closed-form decomposition attributes the accumulated interference to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions, showing that the two constraints suppress these respective sources. Across continual erasure of celebrities, artistic styles, and instances, CEASE achieves the most consistent erase--preserve trade-off, while existing methods either degrade general generation or insufficiently erase targets. 1 1 1 Project page: https://continual-erasure.cvmlgroup.web.illinois.edu/ 1 Introduction Concept erasure aims to remove copyright-protected, privacy-sensitive, or otherwise undesirable concepts from pretrained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models, making it an important tool for content governance and compliance Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2025) . In practice, new erasure targets arrive over time Lee et al. (2026) ; George et al. (2025) , extending concept erasure from one-shot to continual editing: the model must remove new targets without allowing later updates to undo prior erasures or degrade generation of unrelated concepts. Prior studies report that retained model utility declines when erasure requests are processed sequentially Lee et al. (2026) ; George et al. (2025) . In our experiments, sequentially applying standard erasure methods Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2026) reveals two related failure modes. First, general generation quality declines on prompts unrelated to any erased concept. Second, outputs for some erased targets become incoherent instead of reflecting the prescribed replacement ( e.g. “a person” for a celebrity). Each edit explicitly protects only a finite retain set Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2026) and can therefore perturb embeddings outside it Wuerkaixi et al. (2025) ; Thakral et al. (2025) . These perturbations interact and accumulate across successive updates, making it difficult for existing methods Li et al. (2026) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) to confine the effects of erasure to the target concepts. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), COCO FID on unrelated prompts rises as the number of edits increases Lin et al. (2014) . This exposes a limitation of existing preservation constraints in the continual setting: protecting a finite retain set at each step does not reliably prevent subsequent updates from cumulatively degrading general generation. Beyond image quality, this degradation also weakens the model’s ability to follow prompt semantics: Figure 1 (b) shows that, after 100 edits, the CLIP score on the same prompts falls well below that of the unedited model. This reduced ability to follow prompt semantics may also affect the outcomes of previous erasures, because the replacement outputs for earlier targets depend on the same continually updated weights. Figure 1 (c) illustrates both effects in the baseline models: they corrupt an unrelated scene and produce noise for the erased celebrity, failing to generate the prescribed generic portrait. Figure 1: Utility loss under continual celebrity erasure. (a) COCO FID on 1,000 unrelated prompts as the number of erased concepts grows from 10 to 100; lower is better. (b) COCO CLIP score on the same prompts after 100 edits; the dashed line marks the unedited model. (c) Generations after 100 edits for an unrelated COCO scene (top) and the erased target “Tom Cruise” (bottom). To suppress the accumulation of interference in continual concept erasure, we propose CEASE ( C ontinual E rasure via A daptive S ubspace E diting), a training-free method based on two subspace constraints. CEASE adds the token representation of the shared replacement to the invariance matrix of the closed-form solver, preventing subsequent updates from modifying this representation. It also extracts the dominant output directions from cumulative past updates and, when interference is detected, projects the current update onto their orthogonal complement. Theoretically, a closed-form decomposition attributes the accumulated interference to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions, and shows that the two designs suppress the respective sources. Empirically, CEASE maintains stable COCO FID throughout the edit sequence and a COCO CLIP score close to the unedited reference after 100 edits, as shown in Fig. 1 (a) and (b). Across continual erasure tasks involving celebrities, artistic styles, and instances, CEASE achieves the most consistent erase–preserve trade-off. On style erasure, CEASE reduces COCO FID by 73% relative to the strongest prior method. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We formalize how interference accumulates across edits in continual concept erasure, and derive a closed-form decomposition that attributes it to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions. • We introduce two training-free subspace constraints: one keeps the token representation of the shared replacement invariant, while the other steers the current update away from the dominant output directions of past edits, thereby suppressing the two interference sources. • We evaluate continual erasure of celebrities, artistic styles, and instances across multiple diffusion backbones and assess both erasure and preservation; CEASE achieves the best erase–preserve balance among the compared methods while keeping retained concepts recognizable at rates close to the reference model. 2 Related Work Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models. Text-to-image diffusion models Zhang et al. (2023a) ; Ma et al. (2024) ; Ji et al. (2026) trained on uncurated web data can reproduce copyrighted styles, recognizable identities, and other undesired content, and concept erasure removes such targets from a pretrained model after training. Existing methods fall into three families. Training-based methods fine-tune the model with a concept-suppression objective and a preservation regularizer Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2024) ; Kumari et al. (2023) ; Huang et al. (2024) ; Lyu et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Kim et al. (2024) ; Zhao et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2025) , with a separate strand hardening the erasure against adversarial prompts Fan et al. (2024) ; Heng and Soh (2023) ; Pham et al. (2024) ; Park et al. (2024) ; their common cost is that each new target requires another fine-tuning loop. Editing-based methods instead update cross-attention projections through a closed-form least-squares solution, from TIME Orgad et al. (2023) and UCE Gandikota et al. (2024) to MACE Lu et al. (2024) , RECE Gong et al. (2024) , and SPEED Li et al. (2026) ; they edit the model in seconds, but their preservation depends on a finite retain set. Non-parametric methods leave the weights untouched and intervene at sampling time Schramowski et al. (2023) ; Das et al. (2024) ; Rando et al. (2022) . All three families are typically evaluated with the full target set known before editing; our study instead evaluates repeated application to an already-edited model. Sequential Unlearning. Sequential unlearning is closely related to continual learning and online learning Liu et al. (2020) ; Liu et al. (2021a) ; Liu et al. (2021b) ; Liu et al. (2023a) ; Liu et al. (2023b) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2019) ; Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Fischer et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2023b) . While continual learning and online learning typically focus on acquiring new knowledge without forgetting, sequential unlearning poses the complementary challenge of repeatedly removing targeted knowledge without causing unintended forgetting of retained concepts. In deployment, takedown demands and right-to-be-forgotten obligations arrive as a stream. For language models, the locate-then-edit paradigm Meng et al. (2022a) ; Meng et al. (2022b) degrades under repeated application, and mitigations include drift-restraining regularizers Ma et al. (2025) ; Gu et al. (2024) , external edit memories Hartvigsen et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2024b) , and projections onto the null space of preserved keys Fang et al. (2025) ; these approaches operate on factual associations, where edits do not share a common redirection target. For diffusion models, Selective Amnesia Heng and Soh (2023) first cast concept forgetting as a continual-learning problem, and later work adds concept-aware masking with distillation Li et al. (2025) , gradient projection against semantically related concepts Lee et al. (2026) , and multi-objective distillation across deletion requests George et al. (2025) ; these methods suppress the degradation as a monolithic quantity without analyzing where it comes from. In contrast, we approach continual erasure from the perspective of cross-edit interference: we trace the failure to the interference that successive edits accumulate on unprotected prompts, and design our method to suppress this interference. 3 Analysis and Method Section 3.1 defines the continual erasure problem and the base closed-form update. In addition, we analyze the robustness of CEASE to the erasure order in Appendix A.5 , and compare its computational efficiency with all baselines in Appendix A.6 . 5 Conclusion We studied continual concept erasure, where deletion requests arrive one after another and each edit builds on all previous ones. We traced the severe degradation of existing methods in this regime to accumulating cross-edit interference, and proposed CEASE, a training-free framework that protects the shared anchor and steers each new update away from the directions perturbed by past edits. Experiments on erasing celebrities, artistic styles, and instances across multiple backbones show that CEASE achieves the most consistent erase–preserve trade-off. Limitations. First, our experiments focus on the Stable Diffusion family, and extending CEASE to more recent architectures such as FLUX is a natural next step. Second, this work instantiates the proposed constraints in a closed-form solver, and generalizing them to training-based erasure methods is left to future work. Third, our sequences contain up to 100 edits; evaluating substantially longer streams is conceptually straightforward but computationally expensive, since every additional step requires regenerating and re-evaluating thousands of images.
